cards.title: THE PRIMARY BATHROOM
cards.tagline: SEVEN ZONES. START WITH THE COUNTER.
cards.objective: The primary bathroom is the smallest room you use the most, and it carries three problems no other room has all at once: standing moisture, open chemistry, and dates that quietly pass while you sleep. This card is the map and the order.
zones_in_order: PBZ-004 Medicine Cabinet or Wall Storage
cards.start_here: PBZ-001 Vanity Counter. Counter first, shower second. Those two are what you stand in front of every morning, and finishing them makes the under-sink cabinet worth opening. Leave the medicine cabinet for a session where you are willing to read small print on the back of a box.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the seven ZONE cards face up. Pick the one that is annoying you today, or take the one this card says to start at.
2. Lay out that zone's three FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true in your bathroom. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 4. With more than one, split the chain: one clears the counter and drawers, another works the cabinet and the shower.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do PBA-016 The Open-Chemistry Check before any rebuild. It takes thirty minutes and covers what makes this room different from every other: chemicals, water and electricity, and dates that pass while you sleep.

cards.done_looks_like: One tray you can lift with one hand, holding soap, the toothbrush holder, and no more than four daily products. Bare stone on both sides of the basin, a mirror with no splatter, and no cord crossing the sink.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: A plugged-in heat tool sitting within cord reach of a full basin. Nothing stays plugged in while there is water standing in the bowl.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: A hot iron set down on a towel or a cosmetic bag to cool. Give it a metal or ceramic rest it always returns to, in the same spot every time.

the_call.title: The tool that lives out
the_call.text: The straightener or the dryer sits on the counter because the outlet is right there and you use it three or four times a week. That convenience is exactly what is costing you a clear counter, and it is the decision you keep stepping around. The rule that settles it: the counter holds only what you touch every single day. Three times a week is a drawer tool, so buy the heat-safe pouch, give it a drawer, and accept the few seconds it costs you. If the drawer genuinely will not reach from where you stand to dry your hair, the honest fix is a wall-mounted holder beside the mirror, not the counter.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle

the_call.title: The expensive shade you never wear
the_call.text: There is a palette or a bottle in there that cost more than you like to remember, and you have used it twice. Keeping it is not thrift, it is paying storage on a decision that already went wrong, and you skip past it on every Sort pass because binning it means admitting the money is gone. The money is gone either way. The rule: if it is open and past its window, or you reached for something else the last three times, it leaves today. If it is unopened and still in date, it gets one season, and you write that season on a strip of tape stuck to the base so the clock is visible instead of imaginary.

cards.objective: To store cleaning supplies and backstock around the plumbing without ever hiding a leak.

cards.done_looks_like: Two pull-out bins clear of the P-trap, a pale tray on the cabinet floor with nothing stacked on it, one open bottle per job, and both shut-off valves in plain sight when the doors swing open.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Bleach, drain opener, and bowl cleaner sitting at a crawling child's eye level behind one unlatched door. Fit a catch or move them above the sink line.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: A drip at the trap creeping toward a socket or a plugged-in nightlight on the wall behind the cabinet. Find it, and fix it now.

the_call.title: The pipe you cannot see
the_call.text: You have packed this cabinet wall to wall because it is the only storage in the room, and the P-trap is now buried behind a tower of paper towels. Here is the arithmetic you have been avoiding: a joint that weeps unnoticed for months turns a cheap washer into a rotted cabinet base and a floor that has to come up. The rule: the trap joint and both shut-off valves stay visible whenever the doors are open, and nothing sits on the tray. If that means the backstock will not fit, the backstock leaves this room, not the sightline. Spare shampoo and toilet rolls can live in a linen cupboard. A leak cannot live anywhere else.

Prescriptions grouped by the name on the label, the first aid bin small enough to carry one-handed to whoever is bleeding, and the whole cabinet above a child's reach with a catch on it if children are in the house.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Loose tablets, gummy vitamins, and pushed-through blister packs at a height a child reaches by standing on a closed toilet lid. Measure the reach from what they can climb, not from the floor.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A glass peroxide bottle or a heavy first aid tin balanced on the top shelf above a hard basin. Heavy and breakable belongs at eye level, not overhead.

the_call.title: The leftover prescription
the_call.text: There is a half-course of antibiotics in here, or a bottle of strong painkillers from a procedure two years ago, and you keep it because it might come in useful and because handing it back feels like waste. It is the single most common thing in this cabinet that should not be in it. The rule: a medicine belongs to a condition someone in this house has now, prescribed to that person, in date, with the label intact. Everything else goes in the take-back bag today, including the one you are quietly telling yourself is still fine. Leftover painkillers sitting behind a mirror are the most likely thing in this room to seriously hurt a visitor, and nothing about not wasting them outweighs that.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: Soap film on wet glaze, worst at the moment you step over a high tub wall. Grip strips or a mat that truly grips, and a grab bar if anyone in the house is unsteady.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A razor resting on the tub edge at exactly the height a child grabs to steady themselves. High hook, out of reach, every single time.

the_call.title: The bottle you are keeping out of guilt
the_call.text: There are four or five bottles in there you do not use. Some cost too much to admit, some were gifts, and some hold an inch you cannot bring yourself to pour away. Meanwhile the caddy never dries out, the shelf grows a ring, and you shift eight bottles to clean a space that should hold four. The rule: a product is in use if you touched it in the last two weeks of showers. If you did not, it leaves the enclosure today. The inch in the bottom is not saved money, it is what keeps mold on your shelf, so use it this week or pour it out and recycle the bottle. Gifts get no exemption for being gifts.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Bowl cleaner standing at floor level beside the pedestal, and the chance of it meeting bleach in the same bowl. One product per bowl, stored high.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: A phone charger run up to the cistern top so you can sit and scroll. A cord, a water tank, and a hard tile floor is a combination worth ending today.

the_call.title: What you keep within splash range
the_call.text: The cistern lid is the most tempting shelf in the room, and every flush throws a fine mist across it. The decision you have been avoiding is not whether that is true, it is which of your things you are willing to keep there anyway. Settle it with one line: nothing that touches your face, your mouth, or your food goes within arm's reach of the bowl. Toothbrushes, lens cases, hand cream, drinking glasses, and open candles all move out. What may stay is the brush, the lidded bin, the reserve rolls, and cleaner stored high. If that leaves the lid bare, that is the right answer, and it has the useful side effect that the lid finally gets wiped.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: An overloaded shelf on light brackets, or a stack tall enough to topple when you pull a towel from the middle. Check the fixings and keep the heavy bath towels low.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: A step stool on a wet bathroom floor to reach the top shelf. Move the everyday linens down to shelves you can reach flat-footed.

the_call.title: The good towels you never use
the_call.text: You have a set kept back for guests who visit twice a year, and three thin gray towels you reach for every single day because using the good ones feels like spending them. That is a shelf running backwards, and it has been running backwards for years. The rule: rank every towel you own, use the top of that ranking daily, and let the worn ones go now instead of after another year of being the ones you actually touch. Keep exactly one guest set, in a pillowcase, and put everything else into rotation. A towel saved for a better occasion is a towel wearing out in a cupboard while you dry yourself on a rag.

cards.title: CLEAR THE COUNTER TO THE DAILY FOUR
cards.objective: Clear the counter down to bare stone and put back only the tray with the soap, the toothbrush holder and the four products you actually touched today.
cards.why_it_matters: A counter with no boundary on what belongs is why it fills back up within two days, and 'I might use it' is not the same test as 'I used it today.'
steps: Take everything off the counter, wipe the bare stone and the mirror, then put back only the soap, the toothbrush holder and the four products you touched today.
Coil or unplug any cord that crosses the basin.
Move any glass bottle back off the counter edge to the row against the mirror.
If this counter is shared, give each person their own tray rather than one merged pile.

cards.title: GIVE THE HEAT TOOL A DRAWER OR A WALL HOOK

cards.why_it_matters: The straightener sitting out because the outlet is close is the single biggest reason the counter never stays clear, and stepping around that decision every day costs more than the few seconds a drawer costs.
inputs: or a wall-mounted holder if the drawer will not reach
steps: Decide honestly whether you use the tool three or four times a week, which is a drawer tool, or daily, which stays on the counter as the one item.
If it's a drawer tool, buy or repurpose a heat-safe pouch and give it a fixed spot in the vanity drawer.
If the drawer genuinely will not reach from where you stand to dry your hair, fit a wall-mounted holder beside the mirror instead.
Confirm the tool has a rest it returns to every single time, on the counter or off it.
cards.victory_condition: The heat tool has one fixed home, either a labeled drawer pouch or a wall-mounted holder, and the counter no longer needs it to explain why it is not clear.

steps: Empty the top drawer onto a towel, bin anything past its open-jar window, cap the blades into one lidded box, and put back only what you reach for daily, each in its own compartment.

cards.title: JUDGE THE EXPENSIVE SHADE BY THE THREE-STRIKE RULE
cards.objective: Work through every open product against the reach-for-something-else test, and write the season on anything unopened you're keeping.
cards.why_it_matters: Keeping an expensive product you don't use is not thrift, it's paying storage on a decision that already went wrong, and skipping the drawer on every Sort pass only lets it happen again.
inputs: a strip of tape and a marker
steps: Pull every open product in the drawers and ask: did I reach for something else the last three times instead of this?
If yes and it's past its window, it leaves today, no exceptions for cost.
If it's unopened and in date, write the season on a strip of tape stuck to the base so the clock is visible.
Recheck any taped item at the next season's Sort pass and give it a real verdict then.
cards.victory_condition: Every open product in the drawers has been reached for in the last three uses, and every kept unopened one carries a visible season on tape.

inputs: space identified in a linen cupboard
steps: Pull out everything beyond the two open-bottle bins.
Sort what's left into 'this belongs in the linen cupboard' and 'this is genuinely bathroom-only backstock.'

cards.title: SORT INTO THREE LABELED BINS
cards.objective: Empty the cabinet, clear anything expired, and sort what remains into three labeled bins.
cards.why_it_matters: A leftover prescription kept 'in case' is the single most common thing in here that shouldn't be, and expired pain relief mixed with first aid costs you time in the one moment you can't afford to lose any.
steps: Take everything out, bin anything past its date, and sort what is left into three labeled bins: pain relief, stomach and cold, first aid.
Group any prescriptions together by the name on the label.
Confirm the first aid bin is light enough to carry one-handed.

cards.title: CONFIRM THE REACH AND FIT THE CATCH
cards.objective: Measure the cabinet's real height against what a child can climb to reach, and fit a catch if children are ever in the house.

a step stool to test the reach yourself
steps: Stand on the closed toilet lid yourself and check what you can reach: that is a child's real reach in this room, not the floor-to-shelf distance.
Move anything glass or heavy off any shelf within that reach.
Fit a catch or child lock on the cabinet door if children are ever in the house.
Confirm the whole cabinet, catch included, is checked working before you close it.

cards.title: DOWN TO ONE OF EACH, THEN SQUEEGEE DRY
cards.objective: Clear the caddy to one shampoo, one conditioner, one wash and one bar per person, and squeegee the whole enclosure dry.

inputs: a bag for empties or recycling
steps: Take every bottle out, bin the empties, keep one shampoo, one conditioner, one wash and one bar per person in the caddy, then squeegee the walls and the tray dry.
Hang the squeegee back on its hook inside the enclosure.

cards.objective: Test every bottle against the two-week rule, and settle the inch in the bottom of anything you're keeping out of guilt.
cards.why_it_matters: The inch you can't bring yourself to pour away is what keeps mold on the shelf, and a gift gets no exemption for being a gift once it stops being used.
steps: Line up every bottle in the shower and ask: did I touch this in the last two weeks of showers?
Anything you didn't touch leaves the enclosure today, gift or not.

Recheck the caddy count against the one-per-person standard once the pass is done.

cards.title: THE OPEN-CHEMISTRY CHECK
cards.objective: Walk the room checking that no two products stored near each other could ever mix badly, and that nothing corrosive sits within a child's reach.
